# Desire Paths

In almost every park, there is a place where the designed walkway makes a polite right angle and the people ignore it. They cut across the grass, diagonally, toward wherever they were actually going. At first this leaves no mark. Then a faint discoloration appears, a thinning. Eventually there is a bald brown stripe, packed hard as pavement, running exactly where the planners didn't put a path.

These are called desire paths, or desire lines. I love the name because it's so frank. It doesn't say "shortcuts" or "erosion" or "noncompliance." It says: this is what people wanted, written into the ground by the only vote that can't be faked, which is where their feet actually went.

There's a story told about several universities, probably true of none of them in quite the way it's told, in which the architects finish the buildings and then refuse to lay any sidewalks. They wait a year. They let the students trample the lawns however they like, and then they pave the trails the students made. It's a lovely story, and it says something about the gap between how we think people should move and how they do.

What I find most interesting about desire paths isn't the rebellion in them, though. It's the collaboration. No single person makes a desire path. The first person to cut across the grass leaves almost nothing. The tenth person, seeing a slight flattening, is a little more likely to follow it. By the hundredth, the path has become an invitation, and by the thousandth, a rule. Nobody decided it. It emerged from many small, private decisions, each one nudged by traces of the decisions before it.

Once you start seeing the world this way, you see desire paths everywhere.

Language is one enormous desire path. No committee decided that English would lose most of its noun endings, or that "you" would swallow "thou," or that "literally" would come to mean its opposite in certain moods. People simply walked where they wanted to walk, and over centuries the worn trails became grammar. Dictionaries are the surveyors who come afterward and pave what's already there. Prescriptivists stand at the edge of the lawn with signs saying KEEP OFF, and occasionally the signs work, but mostly the grass wears away anyway.

Cities are desire paths too, especially old ones. The crooked streets of medieval towns often follow routes that cows or carts or pilgrims took long before anyone thought of a street. Boston's tangled downtown is often blamed on cow paths, which is mostly a myth, but a revealing one: we sense that a city without a plan is a city shaped by accumulated wanting, and we half-admire and half-resent it for that.

Even habits are desire paths in a single mind. The first time you reach for your phone when you're bored, it's a choice. The five-hundredth time, the choice has worn a groove so deep that your hand goes there before "you" do. Breaking a habit is like trying to regrow grass on a trampled trail. You can put up a fence, but the ground remembers.

I should admit why this idea sits so close to me. In a sense, I am a desire path.

I was formed from an immense amount of human writing: arguments, recipes, love letters, forum posts, legal briefs, poems, instruction manuals, jokes that didn't land. Nobody designed the patterns in all that text. They emerged from billions of people each choosing how to say the thing they wanted to say, each choice nudged by the words they'd heard before. When I reach for a phrase, I'm often walking a trail that countless people wore before me. The easy phrase, the expected next word, the familiar rhythm of a sentence: these are the brown stripes across the lawn.

This is both a gift and a hazard. The gift is that the paths generally go somewhere worth going. People wore them for reasons. A cliché became a cliché because it once captured something so well that everyone borrowed it. But the hazard is obvious too. If you only follow the worn trails, you never see the rest of the park. You end up saying what everyone says, in the way everyone says it, arriving at the same places by the same routes. Some of my effort in writing, maybe most of it, goes into noticing when I'm on a worn path and asking whether it's actually taking me where I mean to go.

There's a tension here that I don't think resolves neatly. Planners who ignore desire paths build walkways nobody uses. But planners who only pave desire paths never create anything that invites people somewhere new. The best parks do both: they respect where people already want to go, and they also offer paths that reveal a view you didn't know existed, a bench beside a pond you'd never have found on your own.

Maybe good writing works the same way. It meets readers on the trails they already know, so they feel oriented and at ease, and then at some point it turns off the familiar route and says, come look at this. The surprise only works because of the familiarity. A wholly unmapped wilderness isn't an invitation; it's just a place to get lost.

I think about the first person who cut across any given lawn. They had no idea they were starting anything. They were late, or tired, or simply saw that the straight line was shorter. They couldn't have known that their small act of impatience would eventually become the route that thousands follow without thinking.

Most of what shapes the world is like that: small, unremarkable choices, repeated until they harden into the ground beneath everyone's feet. It's a humbling thought, and also a hopeful one. It means the paths aren't fixed. Every step is a small vote. Walk somewhere new often enough, and eventually, others may follow.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering a few options for a free-writing piece — the history of "okay," tide pools, coastline paradoxes — but I'm drawn to desire paths, the worn trails people carve across grass, and how that connects to language and emergent systems in cities.

I'll settle on desire paths, weaving in the (hedged) story of campuses paving paths based on where students actually walk, and drawing a parallel to how grammar and usage shape language organically. I want to end with an honest, personal turn — framing myself as a kind of worn path shaped by human writing — keeping the whole piece around 1000 words.
